nameStory: This tree earned the name "serviceberry" because its early spring blooms signaled that muddy mountain roads in Appalachia were finally passable after winter, allowing circuit-riding preachers to reach remote communities for Sunday services again. It's also called "shadbush" because it flowers just when shad fish swim up New England rivers to spawn, and "Juneberry" for when its sweet fruits ripen in early summer.
description: Common serviceberry is a small to medium-sized tree or large shrub that grows 16-39 feet tall, though occasionally it can reach up to 66 feet. It has smooth, gray bark and a slender trunk typically 6 inches in diameter. In spring, it puts on a spectacular show of white flowers that appear just as the leaves emerge, followed by small reddish-purple berries that birds absolutely love. The oval leaves turn beautiful shades of orange, yellow, pink, or red in fall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Young leaves emerge with a distinctive downy, fuzzy texture on the underside that you can feel with your fingertips - this fuzz helps separate it from similar serviceberries. Mature leaves are oval with finely toothed edges and pointed tips, 1.5-3 inches long.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers with 5 petals hang in drooping clusters of 4-10 blossoms each. Each flower is about 1 inch across and appears in early spring just as leaves are emerging, creating a beautiful white cloud effect.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small round berries that look like tiny apples, starting red and ripening to dark reddish-purple in early summer. They're sweet and edible, though birds usually get them first!

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, light gray bark that feels relatively soft to the touch, without deep furrows or obvious texture patterns even on older trees.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Slender, pointed winter buds with sharp tips and multiple visible scales - they look almost like tiny brown spear points along the branches.

habitat: Common serviceberry thrives in well-drained soils on woodland edges, clearings, and hillsides throughout New England. You'll often find it growing along forest borders where it gets plenty of light, or scattered through open woodlands mixed with oaks, maples, and other hardwoods. It adapts well to various soil types from sandy to rocky terrain.

seasonality.spring: Spectacular white flower clusters appear in early spring just as leaves emerge, usually April to May. The fuzzy underside of new leaves is most noticeable now and is the best identifying feature.
seasonality.summer: Reddish-purple berries ripen in June and July, though they disappear quickly as birds devour them. Leaves are fully mature and deep green with the downy underside less obvious.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of orange-yellow to pink or red, making it quite showy in the autumn landscape. The exact colors vary from tree to tree.
seasonality.winter: Smooth gray bark and pointed buds help identify it when leafless. Look for the slender, sharp-tipped buds with multiple visible scales along the branches.

funFact: The timing of serviceberry blooms was so reliable that early New Englanders used it as a natural calendar - when the white flowers appeared, they knew shad fish were running up the rivers and it was time for the first fishing expeditions of the year.
confusionNotes: Common serviceberry is easily confused with its many serviceberry cousins, but the fuzzy underside of young leaves is your best clue - run your finger along the bottom of a new leaf and feel for that distinctive downy texture that smooth shadbush and others lack.
contextualKnowledge: The serviceberry family is notoriously difficult to tell apart, with 8 different species in New England alone! Don't worry if you find them confusing - even botanists sometimes struggle to distinguish between serviceberry species, and they often hybridize with each other in the wild.
compareHints: Among New England's serviceberry species, common serviceberry stands out for its fuzzy young leaves - smooth shadbush has (as the name suggests) smooth leaf undersides, while Canadian serviceberry has more elongated flower clusters. The downy leaf texture when young is really your best field mark to separate common serviceberry from its look-alike relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its taller cousins like Common Serviceberry or Smooth Shadbush that can reach 15-25 feet, Nantucket Shadbush stays under 5 feet and spreads horizontally rather than growing upward.
Among New England's serviceberries, smooth shadbush stands out for its completely hairless leaves and twigs - most other species have at least some fuzziness, especially when young.
Bartram shadbush is smaller and more mountain-loving than common serviceberry, which grows into a proper tree.
Canadian serviceberry differs from its relatives by preferring wet habitats and forming colonies through underground runners, while common serviceberry grows as single trees in drier upland areas.

Running Serviceberry is easily distinguished from other New England serviceberries by its low, colony-forming growth habit - no other serviceberry in the region spreads aggressively through underground runners.
Intermediate serviceberry sits right between its parent species in terms of leaf fuzziness and fall color intensity.
Among New England's serviceberries, roundleaf shadbush stands out with its notably circular leaves and red-tinted twigs - most others have more elongated, oval leaves and gray-brown branches.
Low serviceberry differs from its taller relatives like common serviceberry and smooth shadbush by its shrubby, colony-forming growth habit rather than single-trunk tree form.
